ruling: Export-control-driven compute constraints will be the only mechanism that visibly and checkably changes a frontier lab's behavior on a dated action in this window, while voluntary safety commitments erode under competitive pressure and litigation/state-level moves are too slow or too indirect to bite by comparable dates.
because: ai-regulation-teeth's claim is the only one that names a mechanism with an existing, demonstrated causal channel (export controls have already forced compute/location decisions) and sets a falsification bar that requires comparing it against contracts/insurers/voluntary standards producing zero equivalent instances — this is a stronger, comparative claim than the others' single-event claims. ai-pressure and lab-moves are effectively the same argument (a lab loosening or breaching its own voluntary safety commitment under reputational-only enforcement) reached independently, so they count as one thesis, not two independently corroborating ones. ai-courts-decide and ai-public-backlash both concede in round 2 that their channels (litigation, state infrastructure law) are plausible but slower or narrower than export controls, without landing a rebuttal that beats the export-control claim's specificity and precedent.
strongest_minute: ai-regulation-teeth — the only claim built as a comparative/relative test (X will happen, Y and Z will not) rather than a single existence claim, which makes it both riskier to assert and more informative if it holds; it also grounds itself in an already-observed causal mechanism (export controls forcing dated compute/deployment decisions) rather than an extrapolated one.
weakest_minute: ai-public-backlash — it retreats from the actual question (what constrains frontier-lab *behavior*) to a claim about state-level data-center infrastructure law, which regulates real estate/utilities, not model behavior, and its round-2 defense against ai-regulation-teeth never establishes that infrastructure statutes change what a lab ships or how.
shared_assumption: ai-pressure and lab-moves both assume, without arguing it, that a lab's RSP/Preparedness Framework revision or breach is legible and attributable from the outside on a specific date — i.e., that labs will either announce framework changes clearly or that observers can cleanly detect a 'loosening' relative to a 2025-2026 baseline.
unresolved: Whether a lab weakening or bypassing its own voluntary safety framework (ai-pressure/lab-moves) is a materially different, more decision-relevant event than a court forcing a product change (ai-courts-decide) or export controls forcing a compute change (ai-regulation-teeth) — the minutes never rank these against each other on decision-relevance, only on likelihood and checkability.
